title: Signs of the end (Matthew 24:1–31)
hook: wars and rumors on every screen, and a first instruction that isn't a date
tomorrow: nobody knows the hour. so what are you meant to be doing?

segments.voice: The woes ended in a hen with her wings open: how often I would have gathered you. Now Jesus walks out of the Temple.
screen: `HOW OFTEN I WOULD HAVE GATHERED YOU.`

segments.voice: Breaking news, a siren in the background, a video from someone's phone. Some weeks every screen feels like an ending. Leaving the Temple, the disciples point out its buildings, the way people point at a skyline. Jesus answers: "There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down." Later, on the Mount of Olives, they come to him privately with the question people still ask in frightening times. When will these things be? And what will be the sign of his coming, and of the end of the world? Two questions in one breath, the stones and the end, and Christians still read his answer in two ways.
screen: `EVERY SCREEN FEELS LIKE AN ENDING.` → `NOT ONE STONE UPON ANOTHER.` → `WHEN? WHAT SIGN?`

segments.voice: His first words aren't a date. "Take heed that no man deceive you." Then: "ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled: for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet." Famines, earthquakes, nation against nation: "All these are the beginning of sorrows." The love of many will grow cold. "But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved." So what is this chapter about? Christians answer two ways, and each has a real case. Some read much of it as the Temple's fall. Their case: Jesus starts with those very stones, and later says, "This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled." The Temple did fall to Rome later, they point out, just as he said. Others hear a future end, still ahead. Their case: the sun darkened, the Son of man coming on the clouds with power, angels gathering his elect from the four winds. That hasn't happened yet, they say, and it's too large for one city. Some hold a bit of both. Here's what both sides share: the first instructions. Don't be fooled. Don't be troubled. Keep loving while love cools around you. The rumors will keep coming either way.
screen: `TAKE HEED; BE NOT TROUBLED.` · `READING ONE: THE TEMPLE'S FALL.` · `READING TWO: AN END STILL AHEAD.` · `BOTH SHARE THE FIRST WORDS.` · then, large: `BE NOT TROUBLED.`

segments.voice: Find one steady sound near you: a fan, rain, traffic, a refrigerator's hum, your own breath. For this sit, let that one sound be louder than any headline. When the news drifts back in, return to the sound, and let the three words ride on it: be not troubled.
Signs of the end. Jesus' words about the Temple and the end of the age, which open with a warning to stay calm.
Hold onto this: be not troubled, because the end, he says, is not yet. Peace for today.

screen: `DAY 1473 COUNTS.` → `MATTHEW, READ THROUGH · 47 OF 60.` → `TOMORROW: NOBODY KNOWS THE HOUR. SO WHAT ARE YOU MEANT TO DO?`

howItsDone: Christians read Matthew 24 in different ways, as the Temple's fall, a future return of Christ, or both; the Nicene Creed, said in the worship of a number of churches, says Christ shall come again with glory.

fork.setup: you read Matthew 24 as all about a future end. a friend reads it as the Temple's fall, long ago. what's the strongest case for your friend's side?
options: it starts with the Temple's stones, and says this generation shall not pass.
nobody back then cared much what happened to the Temple.
the chapter never mentions anything that could be future.
fork.reveal: the Temple reading leans on 24:2 and 24:34. the future reading leans on the Son of man on the clouds (24:30). both keep the first instruction: be not troubled.

original.note: Greek for age: the disciples ask about the end of the age, 'end of the world' in the KJV (Matthew 24:3).

trapdoor: what you thought: Matthew 24 is a checklist for predicting the end of the world.
what it means: a warning not to be fooled or troubled, read by some as the Temple's fall and by others as a future end.
what a scholar hears: the disciples' question pairs the Temple with 'the end of the age' (αἰών, 24:3); 24:34 anchors the Temple reading, and 24:29–31 echoes Daniel's son of man on the clouds.

chat.says: dad's crew is at the warehouse fire on the news. everyone's posting videos. i can't stop refreshing
options: Text him once, then phone face down. Be not troubled isn't not caring; it's not drowning.
Keep watching every update. Jesus told them to watch, so staying glued to it is right.
Pray hard. Fires and disasters like this one are the signs Jesus said the end is here.
chat.meaning: Jesus doesn't deny that hard news comes; he says see that ye be not troubled, and the end is not yet. Calm is a way to keep loving.

Temple.meaning: the great house of worship in Jerusalem

Mount of Olives.meaning: a hill facing Jerusalem across a valley

Son of man.meaning: a title Jesus uses for himself, echoing Daniel

elect.meaning: the chosen; here, God's people gathered in

notes: Debate shape: two readings inside Christianity (much of it the Temple's fall / a future end), each given its best case, plus 'some hold a bit of both'. Confirm the wording is fair to preterist, futurist and mixed readers.

CLAIM to check: 'The Temple did fall to Rome later, they point out' is voiced as the Temple-reading's case, with no date stated. The cited text (24:2, 24:34) doesn't record the destruction; a scholar should confirm the phrasing is acceptable or soften it.
Verse 24:34 is quoted; it sits just past this day's passage (24:1–31) and is used as the Temple reading's evidence. Tomorrow's lesson (24:32–51) does not repeat it.
Trapdoor/original: 'end of the world' (KJV 24:3) renders συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος. Confirm.
